newsitem.title: GABON: Brazzaville mediator says no deal yet.
newsitem.headline: Brazzaville mediator says no deal yet.

text.p: A mediator seeking a lasting end to political and ethnic bloodshed in the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville said on Monday that the warring parties broadly agreed on many points but a rapid result was unlikely.

U.N. special envoy Mohamed Shanoun said in Gabon's capital Libreville that one side wanted the main sticking point debated in Brazzaville with representatives of society at large. He did not elaborate.

But Sahnoun warned that if the talks between envoys of President Pascal Lissouba and of his estranged predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso failed, the international community would highlight who was responsible for the breakdown.

"We cannot remain passive witnesses to what is happening in Congo," Sahnoun told reporters. "If these negotiations fail to achieve the hoped-for result those who are to blame will be identified and their responsibility highlighted."
But Sahnoun warned against expecting a dramatic breakthrough. "You shouldn't expect spectacular and rapid results. It's like in any mediation."

The U.N. envoy, who helped Gabon's President Omar Bongo end similar clashes that killed at least 2,000 people in Brazzaville in 1993, has once again shuttled between the Congolese and Gabonese capitals.
"I will simply say that, on the whole, these proposals have the assent of the delegations," he said, but he added:
"There is one point on which there are differences and one delegation wants certain of these proposals discussed...more widely in Brazzaville with society at large."
With a fragile truce holding in Brazzaville, the rival delegations in Libreville have yet to meet face-to-face.
Monday's session followed a weekend decision by Congo Republic's Constitutional Council to postpone a July 27 presidential election formally and extend Lissouba's mandate until polling can be held.
It was not immediately clear whether the prolongation of Lissouba's mandate, which expires at the end of August, would be limited to a 90-day period set out in the constitution.
Sassou has been demanding a government of national salvation to run the oil-producing former French colony until elections.
Sahnoun said Bongo had suspended discussions to wait for Lissouba's prime minister, Charles David Ganao, who arrived late on Monday. Both Lissouba and Sassou remained in Brazzaville.
The ceasefire, which took effect in Brazzaville on July 14, has more or less held -- making it the longest truce since the fighting began on June 5.
The showdown began after government troops surrounded Sassou's home as part of a crackdown on private militia ahead of the July 27 election.
Medical workers say hundreds of people have died, many of them civilians killed by indiscriminate shelling.
Plans for a U.N. sponsored, mainly African peacekeeping force are taking shape. Senegal has agreed to command it.
